'''Mileva Marić''' ({{lang-sr-cyr|Милева Марић}}, {{IPA|sr|milěːva mǎːritɕ|pron}}; 19 December 1875 – 4 August 1948), sometimes called '''Mileva Marić-Einstein''' ({{lang-sr-cyr|Милева Марић-Ајнштајн|Mileva Marić-Ajnštajn|label=none}}), was a Serbian mathematician. She was also the first wife of [[Albert Einstein]] from 1903 to 1919. She was the only woman among Einstein's fellow students at [[Zurich Polytechnic]]. Marić and Einstein were study colleagues and lovers, and had a daughter [[Lieserl Einstein|Lieserl]] in 1902, who likely died of [[scarlet fever]] at one and a half years old. They later had two sons, [[Hans Albert Einstein|Hans Albert]] and [[Einstein family#Eduard "Tete" Einstein (Albert's second son)|Eduard]]. The question of whether she contributed to Einstein's early work (in particular the ''[[Annus mirabilis papers|annus mirabilis papers]]'') has been debated.

==Biography==
Marić was born into a wealthy [[Serbs|Serbian]] family on 19 December 1875 in [[Titel]], a town in [[Bács-Bodrog County]], Kingdom of Hungary, Austro-Hungarian Empire. She was the eldest of three children born to Miloš Marić (1846–1922) and Marija Ružić-Marić (1847–1935).<ref>M. Popović (2003). ''In Albert's Shadow: The Life and Letters of Mileva Marić, Einstein's First Wife'', p. xv<br /><!-- Is this a separate citation? -->"The Family Tree of Mileva Marić-Einstein"</ref> 

She began her secondary education in 1886 at a high school for girls in [[Novi Sad]], but changed the following year to the [[Sremska Mitrovica Gymnasium|Mitrovica Gymnasium]] in [[Sremska Mitrovica]].<ref name="Highfield, 1993, pp. 36">Highfield, 1993, pp. 36–43.</ref> Beginning in 1890, Marić attended the Royal Serbian Grammar School in [[Šabac]]. In 1891, her father obtained special permission to enroll Marić as a private student at the all-male Royal Classical High School in [[Zagreb]].<ref name="Highfield, 1993, pp. 36"/> Her mathematics teacher was [[Vladimir Varićak]].<ref>Veljan, D. (2020) "More on Croatian and Zagreb Mathematics", ''[[Mathematical Intelligencer]]'' 42: 49–54  {{doi|10.1007/s00283-019-09928-1}}</ref> She passed the entrance exam and entered the tenth grade in 1892. She won special permission to attend physics lectures in February 1894 and passed the final exams in September 1894. Her highest grades were in mathematics and physics, both "very good", one grade below the highest "excellent".<ref>Esterson and Cassidy, 2019, pp. 10, 269</ref> That year she fell seriously ill and decided to move to Switzerland, where on 14 November she started at the Girls High School in Zurich. In 1896, she passed her [[Matura|Matura-Exam]], and started studying medicine at the [[University of Zurich]] for one semester.<ref name="Highfield, 1993, pp. 36"/>

In the fall of 1896, Marić switched to the Zurich Polytechnic (later ''Eidgenössische Technische Hochschule'', [[ETH]]), having passed the mathematics entrance examination with an average grade of 4.25 (scale 1–6).<ref name="Trbuhuvić">D. Trbuhuvić-Gjurić, ''Im Schatten Albert Einsteins'', 1988, pp. 35, 43, 49, 60, 63</ref> She enrolled for the diploma course to teach physics and mathematics in secondary schools (section VIA) at the same time as Albert Einstein. She was the only woman in her group of six students, and the fifth woman to enter that section. Marić and Einstein became close friends quite soon. In October, Marić went to [[Heidelberg]] to study at [[Heidelberg University]] for the winter semester of 1897/98, attending physics and mathematics lectures as an auditor. She rejoined the Zurich Polytechnic in April 1898,<ref name="Highfield, 1993, pp. 36"/> where her studies included the following courses: [[Differential calculus|differential]] and [[Integral|integral calculus]], [[Descriptive geometry|descriptive]] and [[projective geometry]], [[mechanics]], [[theoretical physics]], [[applied physics]], [[experimental physics]], and [[astronomy]].<ref name="Trbuhuvić"/>

She sat for the intermediate [[diploma]] examinations in 1899, one year later than the other students in her group. Her grade average of 5.05 (scale 1–6) placed her fifth out of the six students taking the examinations that year.<ref name="Trbuhuvić"/> Marić's grade in physics was 5.5 (the same as Einstein's). In 1900, she failed the final teaching diploma examinations with a grade average of 4.00, having obtained only grade 2.5 in the mathematics component (theory of functions).<ref>{{cite arXiv <!-- unsupported parameter |url=https://arxiv.org/ftp/arxiv/papers/1503/1503.08020.pdf --> |title=(PDF) The Collaboration of Mileva Maric and Albert Einstein|eprint=1503.08020|last1=Asmodelle|first1=Estelle|year=2015|class=physics.hist-ph}}</ref>

Marić's academic career was disrupted when she became pregnant by Einstein on a short holiday in Italy in May 1901. When three months pregnant, she resat the diploma examination, but failed for the second time without improving her grade.<ref>Stachel (1996), pp. 41, 52, n. 22</ref> She discontinued work on her diploma dissertation that she had hoped to develop into a PhD thesis under the supervision of the physics professor [[Heinrich Friedrich Weber|Heinrich Weber]] and returned home to Serbia to birth and care for their daughter.<ref>Highfield, 1993, p. 80</ref>

==Debate over collaboration with Einstein==
[[File:Albert Einstein and his wife Mileva Maric.jpg|thumb|Albert and Mileva Einstein, 1912]]

The question whether (and if so, to what extent) Marić contributed to [[Albert Einstein]]'s early work, and to the [[Annus mirabilis papers|''annus mirabilis'' papers]] in particular, is a subject of debate. Many historians of physics argue that she made no significant scientific contribution,<ref>Pais, A. (1994), pp. 1–29</ref><ref>Holton, G. (1996), pp. 177–93</ref><ref>Stachel, J. (2002), pp. 26–39, 55</ref><ref>Martinez, A. (2005)</ref><ref>Calaprice, A. & T. Lipscombe (2005), pp. 41–42</ref> while others suggest that she was a supportive companion in science and may have helped him materially in his research,<ref>Maurer, M. (1996); Troemel-Ploetz, S. (1990)</ref><ref>Walker, E.H. (1991){{page needed|date=May 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Ruth H. Howes |author2=Caroline L. Herzenberg |title=Their Day in the Sun|publisher=Temple University Press|year=1999|page=26|isbn=978-1-56639-719-3}}</ref> and there is also a possibility of them developing the scientific concepts together when they were still students.<ref name="Pauline Gagnon">{{Cite web|last=Gagnon|first=Pauline|date=19 December 2016|title=The Forgotten Life of Einstein's First Wife|url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/guest-blog/the-forgotten-life-of-einsteins-first-wife/|access-date=17 October 2020|website=Scientific American Blog Network|archive-date=17 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201017222145/https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/guest-blog/the-forgotten-life-of-einsteins-first-wife/|url-status=live}}</ref> 

=== Debate over co-authorship ===
Debate over whether Marić was a co-author of some of Einstein's early work, putatively culminating in the 1905 papers, is based on a passage from Russian physicist [[Abram Joffe]]'s personal memoirs:

{{Blockquote | text=In 1905, three articles appeared in the 'Annalen der Physik', which began three very important branches of 20th century physics. Those were the theory of [[Brownian motion]], the [[Photon#Historical development|photon theory of light]], and the [[theory of relativity]]. The author of these articles – an unknown person at that time, was a bureaucrat at the Patent Office in Bern, Einstein-Marity (Marity the maiden name of his wife, which by Swiss custom is added to the husband's family name). }}

Proponents claim that Joffe was erroneously attributing the addition of the name Marity, Marić's official name, to a "non-existent" [[Double-barrelled_name#Continental_Germanic_tradition|Swiss custom]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Ioffe |first=Abram Fedorovich |author-link=Abram Ioffe |date=1955 |title=Памяти Альберта Эйнштейна |language=ru |trans-title=In memory of Albert Einstein |journal=[[Успехи физических наук]] |volume=57 |issue=10 |issn=0042-1294 |doi=10.3367/UFNr.0057.195510b.0187 |doi-access=free |pages=187–192 |url=https://ufn.ru/ufn55/ufn55_10/Russian/r5510b.pdf}}</ref> Others have argued that it is unlikely Joffe saw the papers before they were published, and also unlikely he would have remembered the exact name on the papers if he did.<ref>Stachel (2005), {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20091111105146/http://www.esterson.org/Stachel_Joffe.htm pp. lxv–lxxii]}}</ref><ref>Martinez, A. (2005), pp. 51–52</ref>

Mileva told a Serbian friend, referring to 1905, that "we finished some important work that will make my husband world famous."<ref>[https://www.pbs.org/opb/einsteinswife/milevastory/married.htm "Mileva's Story"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150430064318/http://www.pbs.org/opb/einsteinswife/milevastory/married.htm |date=30 April 2015 }}, ''Einstein's Wife'', PBS.org; accessed 3 February 2017.</ref> Historians Roger Highfield and Paul Woodson argue that this statement is "hometown folklore".<ref>Highfield and Carter (1993), p. 110</ref>

=== Debate over collaboration ===
Some of the debate over whether Marić collaborated with Einstein is based on their letters:
*[[John Stachel]] argues that letters in which Einstein referred to "our" theory and "our" work were written in their student days, at least four years before the 1905 papers. Stachel also suggests that some of the instances in which Einstein used "our" in relation to scientific work referred to their diploma dissertations, for which they had each chosen the same topic (experimental studies of [[Thermal conduction|heat conduction]]).<ref>Stachel (2002), p. 45.</ref>{{sfn|Finkbeiner|2019}}  Stachel argues that Einstein used "our" in general statements, while he invariably used "I" and "my" when he recounted "specific" ideas he was working on: "the letters to Marić show Einstein referring to 'his' studies, 'his' work on the [[On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies|electrodynamics]] of moving bodies over a dozen times... as compared to 'one' reference to 'our' work on the problem of relative motion."<ref>Stachel (2002), p. 36;<br />The letter dated 27 March 1901 from Einstein says in translation: "How happy and proud I will be, when we two together have victoriously led our work on relative motion to an end!"</ref>
*Stachel also suggests that in two cases where letters from Marić survive that directly respond to those from Einstein in which he had recounted his latest ideas, she gives no response at all. Her letters, in contrast to Einstein's, contain only personal matters, or comments related to her Polytechnic coursework. Stachel writes: "In her case, we have ''no'' published papers, ''no'' letters with a serious scientific content, either to Einstein nor to anyone else; nor any ''objective'' evidence of her supposed creative talents. We do not even have hearsay accounts of conversations she had with anyone else that have a specific, scientific content, let alone claiming to report her ideas."<ref>Stachel (2002), pp. 33–37</ref><ref>Holton, G. (1996), pp. 181–93.</ref> 
Thus, while some scholars have argued that there is not enough evidence to support the idea that Marić helped Einstein to develop his theories,<ref>Holton (1996), pp. 177–93</ref><ref>Stachel (2002), pp. 26–39, 55</ref><ref>Martinez, A.A., ''Mileva Marić''{{full citation needed|date=May 2026}}</ref>{{sfn|Finkbeiner|2019}} others have argued that their letters suggest a collaboration between them, at least through 1901 before their children were born.<ref name="Pauline Gagnon" />

Some of the debate over whether Marić collaborated with Einstein is based on their interactions:
*Marić's brother and other relatives reported eyewitness accounts of Marić and Albert discussing physics together when they were married.<ref name="Pauline Gagnon" />
*The couple's first son, [[Hans Albert Einstein|Hans Albert]] (born 1904), said that when his mother married Einstein in 1903, she gave up her scientific ambitions.<ref>G.J. Whitrow (ed.), ''Einstein: The Man and His Achievements'', p. 19 (1967)</ref>  But he also said that his parents' "scientific collaboration continued into their marriage," and that he "remembered seeing [them] work together in the evenings at the same table."<ref name="Pauline Gagnon" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Krstić|first=Djordje |title=Mileva & Albert Einstein: their love and scientific collaboration |date=2004 |publisher=Didakta |others=Mayer, Janez, 1948– |isbn=961-6530-08-9 |location=Radovljica |page=7 |oclc=447458003}}</ref>

==Family, personal relationships and death==
[[Image:Гроб Милеве Марић-Ајнштајн.jpg|thumb|upright|Memorial gravestone at the Nordheim Cemetery in Zürich]]
Successfully hiding the illegitimate pregnancy, Marić traveled to Újvidék ([[Novi Sad]]), where Einstein's daughter was born in late January 1902. The couple referred to the baby in their correspondence as Hanserl (a male name) before she was born and [[Lieserl Einstein|Lieserl]] after. At the age of one year, Lieserl suffered from [[scarlet fever]], from which she retained permanent damage.<ref name="Einstein 1914">The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, Volume 5 The Swiss Years: Correspondence, 1902–1914. Edited by Martin J. Klein, A. J. Kox, and Robert Schulmann.{{ISBN|9780691033228}}</ref> Some sources say Lieserl died soon after in 1903,<ref name="Einstein 1992">Einstein, Albert and Marić, Mileva (1992) ''The Love Letters''. Edited by Jürgen Renn & Robert Schulmann. Translated by Shawn Smith. Princeton University Press, Princeton, N.J. {{ISBN|0-691-08760-1}}</ref> but others suggest she was put up for adoption in Serbia.<ref>
{{cite book
|last=Singh
|first=S
|title=Big Bang
|publisher=Harper Perennial
|isbn=978-0-00-715252-0
|year=2005
}}</ref> Einstein never met his daughter.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.uni-heidelberg.de/de/universitaet/heidelberger-profile/historische-portraets/mileva-maric-die-fast-vergessene-einstein |title=Mileva Marić: Die (fast) vergessene Einstein |publisher=Heidelberg University |trans-title=Mileva Marić: The (almost) forgotten Einstein |access-date= 4 April 2022 |archive-date= 16 April 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210416224603/https://www.uni-heidelberg.de/de/universitaet/heidelberger-profile/historische-portraets/mileva-maric-die-fast-vergessene-einstein |url-status= live}}</ref>

[[File:Einstein Haus.jpg|thumb|upright|Center: the ''[[Einsteinhaus]]'' Kramgasse 49 in Bern. On the second floor: the flat where Albert and Mileva Einstein lived from 1903 to 1905]]

In 1903, Marić and Einstein married in [[Bern]], Switzerland, where Einstein had found a job at the [[Federal Office for Intellectual Property]]. In 1904, their first son [[Hans Albert Einstein|Hans Albert]] was born. In the following years, Marić and her husband moved several times, because of his changing teaching positions. They lived in Bern until 1909, then moved to Zürich. In 1910, their second son [[Einstein family#Eduard "Tete" Einstein (Albert's second son)|Eduard]] was born. In 1911, they moved to [[Prague]], where Einstein held a teaching position at [[Charles University]]. A year later, they returned to Zurich, as Einstein had accepted a professorship at his [[alma mater]].

In July 1913, Marić was distressed because of her husband's relocation to Berlin, where he was having an affair with his cousin [[Elsa Einstein]].<ref name="Highfield, 1993, 154">Highfield, 1993, pp. 154–166</ref> In August, the family planned a walking holiday with their sons and [[Marie Curie]] and her two daughters. Marić was delayed temporarily due to Eduard being ill but then joined the party. In September 1913, the Einsteins visited Marić's parents near Novi Sad, and on the day they were to leave for Vienna, Marić had her sons baptised as [[Eastern Orthodox|Orthodox Christians]].<ref name="Highfield, 1993, 154"/> After Vienna, Marić returned to Zurich, while Einstein visited relatives in Germany. After Christmas, she traveled to Berlin to stay with [[Fritz Haber]], who helped her look for accommodation for the Einsteins' impending move in April 1914. The couple both left Zurich for Berlin in late March. On the way, Marić took a swimming holiday with the children in [[Locarno]], arriving in Berlin in mid-April.<ref name="Highfield, 1993, 154"/>

The marriage had been strained since 1912. Marić, who had never wanted to go to Berlin, became increasingly unhappy in the city. In mid-July 1914,<ref name="Departure Berlin">{{cite book |last1=Isaacson |first1=Walter |title=Einstein |url=https://archive.org/details/einsteinhislifeu0000isaa |url-access=registration |date=2007 |publisher=Simon & Schuster |location=New York NY |isbn=978-0-7394-8903-1 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/einsteinhislifeu0000isaa/page/185 185–187]}}</ref> her husband insisted on harsh terms if she were to remain with him.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.einsteinfoundation.de/albert/albert-nr-4-aufbruch/die-bessere-haelfte/ |title=Die bessere Hälfte |trans-title=The better half |publisher=Einsteinfoundation.de |access-date=4 April 2022 |archive-date=21 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121155318/https://www.einsteinfoundation.de/albert/albert-nr-4-aufbruch/die-bessere-haelfte/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Although initially accepting the terms, she reconsidered and on 29 July 1914, the day after [[World War I]] started, she left Germany and took the boys back to Zürich, a separation that was to become permanent. Einstein made a legal commitment to send her an annual maintenance of 5600 [[Reichsmark]] in quarterly installments, just under half of his salary,<ref>(approximately 44000 Euros — 5600 times 7.9 — as per [https://web.archive.org/web/20080605142728/http://fredriks.de/HVV/kaufkraft.htm this extract])</ref><ref>Highfield, 1993, p. 172</ref><ref>Isaacson, 2007, p. 186.</ref> a commitment to which he largely adhered.<ref>Fölsing (1997, pp. 420–421), Isaacson (2007, pp. 234–235), Highfield and Carter (1993, p. 186).</ref>  After the required five years of separation, the couple divorced on 14 February 1919.<ref>Highfield, 1993, p. 188.</ref>

Anticipating that Einstein would soon be awarded a [[Nobel Prize in Physics|Nobel Prize]], their divorce agreement stipulated that Einstein would accept the award, while Maric would receive the money. This happened in 1922.<ref>{{cite web |title=Einstein Works Out Details of His 1919 Divorce from Mileva Marić |url=http://www.shapell.org/manuscript/einstein-divorce-from-mileva-maric-hebrew-university |work=Shapell Manuscript Collection |publisher=Shapell Manuscript Foundation |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160306044226/http://www.shapell.org/manuscript/einstein-divorce-from-mileva-maric-hebrew-university |access-date=18 January 2021 |archive-date=6 March 2016}}</ref> Under the terms of the agreement, the money was to be held in trust for their two boys, while she was able to draw on the interest; she couldn't touch the principal without her ex-husband's permission.<ref>Highfield and Carter, p. 187 ("180,000 Swiss Francs")</ref><ref>''The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein'', Vol. 8, document 562.</ref><ref>''Einstein Collected Papers,'' Vol. 8, Docs. pp. 449, 562.</ref> Based on letters released in 2006 [sealed by Einstein's step-daughter ([[Elsa Einstein|Elsa]]'s daughter), Margot Einstein, until 20 years after her death], [[Walter Isaacson]] reported that Marić eventually invested the Nobel Prize money in three apartment buildings in Zurich to produce income.<ref>Walter Isaacson, ''Time'' 168(3): 50–55, 17 July 2006.</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Einstein Writes About House Bought With Nobel Prize Money |url=http://www.shapell.org/manuscript.aspx?einstein-nobel-prize-money-and-family |work=Shapell Manuscript Collection |publisher=Shapell Manuscript Foundation |access-date=3 February 2017 |archive-date=20 December 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141220000658/http://www.shapell.org/manuscript.aspx?einstein-nobel-prize-money-and-family |url-status=live}}</ref> Marić lived in one, a five-story house at Huttenstrasse 62; the other two were investments.

In 1930, at around age 20, her son Eduard had a breakdown and was diagnosed with [[schizophrenia]]. By the late 1930s, the costs of his care at the [[University of Zürich]]'s psychiatric clinic "[[Burghölzli]]" overwhelmed Marić. She sold the two houses to raise funds for his care and maintenance.<ref>Thomas Huonker,
[http://www.thata.net/thomashuonkerdiagnosemoralischdefektzuerich2003opt.pdf#page=204 ''Diagnose: «moralisch defekt» Kastration, Sterilisation und «Rassenhygiene» im Dienst der Schweizer Sozialpolitik und Psychiatrie 1890–1970'' (2003)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161002015228/http://www.thata.net/thomashuonkerdiagnosemoralischdefektzuerich2003opt.pdf#page=204 |date=2 October 2016 }}, Zürich; accessed 3 February 2017. {{in lang|de}}<!-- ISSN/ISBN needed --></ref> In 1939, Marić agreed to transfer ownership of the Huttenstrasse house where she was living to Einstein to prevent its loss, with Marić retaining [[power of attorney]]. Mileva Marić suffered a severe stroke and died at age 72 on 4 August 1948, in Zürich. She was interred there at Nordheim-Cemetery. Eduard Einstein was institutionalized until his death in 1965.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rU6Fs-aZPKgC&q=mileva+maric+date+of+death&pg=PP23|title=In Albert's Shadow: The Life and Letters of Mileva Marić, Einstein's First Wife|last1=Marić|first1=Mileva|last2=Einstein-Marić|first2=Mileva|last3=Einstein-Maric|first3=Mileva|date=2003|publisher=JHU Press|isbn=978-0-8018-7856-5|language=en|access-date=5 October 2020|archive-date=4 May 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220504185546/https://books.google.com/books?id=rU6Fs-aZPKgC&q=mileva+maric+date+of+death&pg=PP23|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Honours==
[[File:Bista Mileve Marić-Ajnštajn, Studentski grad.JPG|thumb|180px|Bust of Marić in [[University of Novi Sad]]]]
In 2005, Marić was honoured in Zürich by the [[ETH Zurich|ETH]] and the [[Gesellschaft zu Fraumünster]]. A memorial plaque was unveiled on her former residence in Zürich, the house Huttenstrasse 62, in her memory.<ref name="fraumünster-Frauenehrungen1">{{cite web |url=http://www.fraumuenstergesellschaft.ch/#page387 |title=Frauenehrungen |trans-title=Women's honors |publisher=[[Gesellschaft zu Fraumünster]] |language=de |access-date=30 November 2014 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304173854/http://fraumuenstergesellschaft.ch/#page387 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="fraumünster-awardlist">{{cite web |url=http://www.fraumuenstergesellschaft.ch/media/upload/aktivitaten/frauenehrung/frauenehrungen.pdf 
 |title=Frauenehrungen der Gesellschaft zu Fraumünster |trans-title=Women's Honors of the Society of Fraumünster |publisher=Gesellschaft zu Fraumünster |language=de |date=2014 |access-date=30 November 2014  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150207162646/http://www.fraumuenstergesellschaft.ch/media/upload/aktivitaten/frauenehrung/frauenehrungen.pdf |archive-date=7 February 2015 }}</ref><ref>ETH und [[Gesellschaft zu Fraumünster]], Zurich ehren Mileva Einstein-Marić [http://archiv.ethlife.ethz.ch/articles/tages/sechselaeuten05.html „Mitentwicklerin der Relativitätstheorie"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120224061655/http://archiv.ethlife.ethz.ch/articles/tages/sechselaeuten05.html |date=24 February 2012 }}, Sechseläuten 2005. [http://www.unifemmes.ch/docs/bull.oct05.pdf#page=33 Laudatio: Katharina von Salis] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131023061236/http://www.unifemmes.ch/docs/bull.oct05.pdf#page=33 |date=23 October 2013 }}; accessed 3 February 2017. {{in lang|de}}</ref> In the same year, a bust was placed in her high-school town, [[Sremska Mitrovica]]. Another bust is located on the campus of the [[University of Novi Sad]]. A high school in her birthplace of [[Titel]] is named after her.<ref>Tesla Memorial Society of New York Website: [http://www.teslasociety.com/mileva_einstein.htm Mileva Marić-Einstein profile] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170913163345/http://www.teslasociety.com/mileva_einstein.htm |date=13 September 2017 }}, teslasociety.com; accessed 3 February 2017.</ref> Sixty years after her death, a memorial plate was placed on the house of the former clinic in Zürich where she died. In June 2009, a memorial gravestone was dedicated to her at the Nordheim-Cemetery in Zürich where she rests.<ref>[http://www.teslasociety.ch/info/rs ''Unveiling and consecration of memorial gravestone dedicated to Mileva Marić-Einstein''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202054211/http://www.teslasociety.ch/info/rs |date=2 February 2017 }}, Republic of Serbia, Ministry for Diaspora, 14 June 2009.</ref>

In 1995, ''Narodna knjiga'' in [[Belgrade]] published (in Serbian) ''Mileva Marić Ajnštajn'' by Dragana Bukumirović, a journalist with ''[[Politika]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Savić|first1=Svenka |year=2002 |title=The Road to Mileva Marić-Einstein: Private Letters |journal=Belgrade Women's Studies Journal |volume=1|issue=Anniversary Issue 1992/2002 |pages=201–10 |location=Belgrade |publisher=Belgrade Women's Studies Center |access-date=5 May 2011 |url=http://www.zenskestudije.org.rs/01_o_nama/svenka_savic/textovi/the_road_to_mileva_maric.doc |quote=[...] a book written by Dragana Bukumirović, a journalist with ''Politika'', entitled Mileva Marić-Ajnštajn[...]|archive-date=23 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120323144840/http://www.zenskestudije.org.rs/01_o_nama/svenka_savic/textovi/the_road_to_mileva_maric.doc |url-status=live}}</ref>

Three years later, in 1998, [[Vida Ognjenović]] produced a drama, ''Mileva Ajnštajn'', which was translated into English in 2002.<ref>''Mrs. Einstein takes the stage'' ''Lincolnwood Review''.</ref> Ognjenović later adapted the play into a [[libretto]] for the opera ''Mileva'', composed by [[Aleksandra Vrebalov]], which premiered in 2011 in the [[Serbian National Theatre]] in Novi Sad.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.snp.org.rs/wp-content/uploads/static/eng/opera/mileva.html |title=Mileva |publisher=Serbian National Theatre |access-date=30 August 2016 |archive-date=10 May 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170510163736/http://www.snp.org.rs/wp-content/uploads/static/eng/opera/mileva.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.blic.rs/kultura/vesti/premijera-opere-mileva/bs25xrp |title=Premijera opere "Mileva" |trans-title=Premiere of the opera "Mileva" |publisher=blic.rs |date=19 October 2011 |language=sr |access-date=30 August 2016 |archive-date=10 May 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170510090734/http://www.blic.rs/kultura/vesti/premijera-opere-mileva/bs25xrp |url-status=live}}</ref>

==Popular culture==
* In her novel ''The Other Einstein'' (2016), [[Marie Benedict]] gives a fictionalized account of the relationship between Mileva Marić and Albert Einstein.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.publishersweekly.com/978-1-4926-3725-7|title=Fiction Book Review: The Other Einstein by Marie Benedict. Sourcebooks Landmark, $25.99 (304p) ISBN 978-1-4926-3725-7|website=publishersweekly.com|access-date=18 January 2018|archive-date=19 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180119060617/https://www.publishersweekly.com/978-1-4926-3725-7|url-status=live}}</ref>
* In 2017, her life was depicted in the first season of the television series ''[[Genius (2017 TV series)|Genius]]'', which focuses on Einstein's life. She was played by [[Nikki Hahn]], [[Samantha Colley]] and [[Sally Dexter]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://scienceandfilm.org/articles/2893/einsteins-girlfriend-on-national-geographic|title=Einstein's Girlfriend on National Geographic|last=Martinez|first=Alberto A.|date=25 April 2017|website=Sloan Science & Film|access-date=25 April 2017|archive-date=26 April 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170426064026/http://scienceandfilm.org/articles/2893/einsteins-girlfriend-on-national-geographic|url-status=live}}</ref>
*A fictionalized depiction of Mileva Marić (portrayed by Christina Jastrzembska) and her potential contributions to Einstein's work is depicted in the first episode of the second season of the [[Time travel|time-travelling]] superhero television series, [[Legends of Tomorrow|DC's ''Legends of Tomorrow'']]. 
* In 2019, physicist and writer Gabriella Greison applied for the posthumous award of a degree to Mileva Marić at the [[ETH Zurich]]. After 4 months of discussions, the university denied the degree.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.repubblica.it/scienze/2019/11/01/news/milena_maric_laurea_postuma-240029825/?ref=RHRS-BH-I240030342-C6-P2-S1.6-T1 |last=Greison |first=Gabriella |title=Il politecnico di Zurigo nega a Mileva Maric la laurea postuma. "Ma Einstein è stato un pessimo marito" |trans-title=Zurich Polytechnic Denies Mileva Maric Posthumous Degree. "But Einstein Was a Terrible Husband" |date=November 2019 |access-date=3 November 2019 |archive-date=4 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220504185550/https://www.repubblica.it/scienze/2019/11/01/news/milena_maric_laurea_postuma-240029825/?ref=RHRS-BH-I240030342-C6-P2-S1.6-T1 |url-status=live }}</ref>
